piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Cortical thinning and functional reorganization as well as related transcriptomic signatures during early motor recovery following acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke (ABGIS) commonly causes severe motor impairment, yet early spatiotemporal patterns of cortical morphological alterations and functional reorganization alongside the spatially coupled transcriptomic signatures remain unclear. Methods Twenty-six ABGIS patients and thirty-three normal controls (NCs) received multimodal MRI and neurological examinations, and patients were reassessed at 1-month follow-up. Cortical morphological changes and brain functional reorganization were analyzed based on cortical thickness (CT) and functional connectivity (FC). We identified the most discriminative FC features based on machine learning (ML) classification and interpretability analyses, and investigated transcriptomic signatures associated with FC alterations via the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Results No differences in CT were found between baseline ABGIS patients (ABGIS_1) and NCs. Compared with ABGIS_1, follow-up patients (ABGIS_2) exhibited reduced CT in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG.L), left superior parietal lobule (SPL.L), and left supramarginal gyrus (SMG.L). Compared with NCs, ABGIS_1 showed decreased FC from PoCG.L/SPL.L to sensorimotor cortex and occipital cortex. ABGIS_2 presented elevated FC relative to ABGIS_1 between PoCG.L and the right precentral gyrus (PreCG.R), and between SPL.L and the bilateral precentral gyrus as well as right superior occipital gyrus. Longitudinal increases in FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R were positively correlated with improvements in Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores. ML models coupled with interpretability analyses preliminarily demonstrated that FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R made prominent contributions to classification. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that gene sets correlated with FC alterations were mainly enriched in neuronal synaptic structure and synaptic signaling, chromatin regulation, as well as DNA and RNA metabolism. Conclusions This study verifies progressive cortical thinning and adaptive functional reorganization during early motor recovery following ABGIS, with such brain functional alterations paralleling distinct transcriptomic signatures, providing neuropathological and spatial transcriptomic clues for interpreting early motor recovery.

piezas.titulo: Relationship Between Spine Deformity and Motor Control With Neurosensory Asymmetry in Patients With Lenke Type 1 Scoliosis - A Pilot Study.

These patients have no neurological, muscular disturbance or any other diseases. However, modern research reveals subtle central nervous system and sensory differences when comparing patients to healthy controls, with a malfunction of the vestibular system and sensory integration. piezas.titulo: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
piezas.resumenOriginal: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. piezas.titulo: Research progress in Guillain-Barré syndrome following heat stroke
piezas.resumenOriginal: Heatstroke-triggered neurological complications are escalating year by year. Although rare, GBS (Guillain-Barré syndrome, GBS) represents a life-threatening sequel of heat-stroke, arising from severe dysfunction of the nervous system. Its pathophysiology unfolds through a tangled cascade of inflammatory pathways and oxidative stress, culminating in diffuse peripheral neuropathies and mortality. Epidemiologically, Guillain-Barré syndrome following heat stroke displays notable demographic variability, with advanced age and male sex emerging as prominent risk factors. Diagnostic approaches hinge upon an integration of biomarkers (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealing a protein-cell dissociation phenomenon), electrophysiological assessments (e.g., motor and sensory nerve conduction studies, F-wave evaluations, and needle electromyography), and clinical criteria, though standardized definitions remain elusive. Treatment strategies encompass immunotherapy (e.g., intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange), glucocorticoid, respiratory function management, nutritional support, rehabilitation, etc. Cases of Guillain–Barré syndrome secondary to heatstroke have been increasingly reported year by year. Currently, a standardized therapeutic protocol for this complication has yet to be established. This article offers a thorough grounded in current knowledge and practical case rescue experience.

piezas.titulo: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
piezas.resumenOriginal: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. piezas.titulo: Prediction Dynamically Modulates Gain and Width of Population Frequency Tuning in Human Auditory Cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: During perception, the brain must veridically portray sensory representations while simultaneously highlighting unexpected events. According to two-process theory of predictive perception, this balance is achieved via complementary mechanisms: precision-weighted predictions sharpen sensory tuning around expected features, while momentary surprisal scales response gain, dampening expected inputs and amplifying unexpected violations. However, standard approaches to investigate these processes, such as categorical multivariate decoding, primarily capture shifts in overall signal-to-noise, making it difficult to disentangle changes in population tuning width from modulations in response gain. Here, we combine ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) with population receptive field (pRF) modelling and a continuous Bayesian ideal observer to test how expectations dynamically modulate frequency tuning across the human auditory hierarchy. We first established static pRF preferences and tuning widths independently of predictive inference. We then separately compared this static pRF tuning against two dynamically modulated alternatives. The first model evaluated how tone-by-tone precision-weighted predictions dynamically sharpen and broaden pRF tuning width, while the second model evaluated how gain (by amplification and dampening) was modulated by tone-by-tone information-theoretic surprisal. Across primary, belt, and associative auditory cortices, both a sharpening model driven by precision-weighted predictions and a gain model driven by surprisal explained significantly more variance compared to a static baseline model. Counterfactual models inverting these driving features yielded no improvement, ruling out non-specific model mimicry. Additionally, contrasting local and global tonotopic implementations revealed a feature-selective dissociation: whereas precision-weighted predictions locally sharpened pRFs tuned to expected frequencies, surprisal acted as a global broadcast signal that multiplicatively scaled pRF gain across all frequency channels of the tonotopic map. Together, these findings demonstrate that the auditory system continuously balances selectivity for expected structure and responsiveness to surprising input through local sharpening and global gain modulation.

piezas.titulo: No Group Differences in Shoulder Joint Position Sense Between Male Baseball and Female Softball Athletes and Controls in Virtual Reality.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Vision and proprioception are the 2 primary senses integrated to plan and execute upper-limb movements. Virtual reality technology enables the investigation of population-level differences in vision-proprioception integration during a shoulder joint position sense test within a 3-dimensional environment by dissociating vision from proprioception through visual hand offsets. A total of 122 participants (collegiate baseball and softball players and age-, sex-, and throwing side-matched healthy controls) performed a shoulder joint position sense test under accurate and offset visual feedback conditions in virtual reality. Participants demonstrated significantly more negative joint repositioning constant error and larger absolute error under offset vision compared with accurate vision (P .05). The mean vision-proprioception reliance score across all groups was 0.9, with 0 to 1 as the theoretical bounds, indicating strong dominance of vision over proprioception. These findings suggest that when both vision and proprioception are available, individuals across populations exhibit comparable repositioning errors through vision dominant integration. Future studies should further examine proprioception-dominant or sport-specific tasks, such as baseball catching or hitting, to clarify population and limb-side differences in multisensory integration mechanisms.

Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: Science keeps the score: why psychotherapies should not be used as standard treatment for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS)
piezas.resumenOriginal: Misattribution of chronic neurologic conditions to psychiatric and psychological causes has been widely prevalent in clinical practice. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and other autonomic disorders are commonly misdiagnosed with psychiatric and psychological conditions despite decades of scientific evidence to the contrary. Terms like “brain-body,” “trauma-informed” and “neuroplasticity-oriented” therapies are gaining traction among some healthcare practitioners despite no published data that these therapies are effective for POTS. In this article, POTS and its relationship to psychological framework and psychotherapies are discussed, including the negative impact of misdiagnosis, diagnostic delay and various barriers to healthcare that exist for patients. Appropriate evidence-based treatment of POTS, which includes increased fluid and salt intake, compression garments, beta blockers, ivabradine, midodrine, fludrocortisone, pyridostigmine and others, should be instituted promptly. There is a great need to develop diverse and effective therapeutic options to target POTS pathophysiology. Cognitive-behavioral, brain-body and other forms of psychotherapies should not be routinely used or recommended as standard treatment for POTS, but could be used as adjunct treatment options for patients with psychiatric or psychological comorbidities if rigorous trials of these therapies demonstrate improved outcomes.

destilado.texto: No es solo mente: también fisiología autónoma. Frontiers in Neurology afirma que no hay datos publicados que demuestren eficacia de psicoterapia para el síndrome POTS. Así, el tratamiento sigue basado en hidratación, sal, fármacos y compresión, reservando la psicoterapia solo como apoyo cuando haya trastornos mentales concomitantes.

piezas.titulo: Motor cortex facilitates visual action override through the superior colliculus
piezas.resumenOriginal: Unexpected visual events can leave goal pursuit undisturbed or trigger visual action override - an interruption that redirects behaviour towards the stimulus. Using a visual distraction task in freely moving mice, population calcium recordings and causal perturbations identified the lateral motor-related superior colliculus (lSCm) as a key node controlling distractor engagement. Retinal inputs to the sensory-related SC signalled distractors even when mice ignored them. Pre-distractor behaviour and motor cortical activity predicted subsequent engagement, while increased corticocollicular and decreased nigrocollicular activity before distractor onset were consistent with a permissive state for override. Suppressing corticocollicular transmission weakened override without detectably altering task engagement. Single-unit recordings in head-fixed mice revealed response amplification in subsets of lSCm neurons during combined retinal and motor cortical stimulation, despite weak responses to either input alone. Motor cortical input thus facilitates sensory recruitment of collicular action circuits, shaping the balance between action stability and action override during ongoing goal pursuit.
